incidents.title: Product search melts the primary
incidents.brief: The shop's search box runs WHERE title ILIKE '%boots%' on a 40M-row products table. At 3,000 searches/s the primary sits at 96% CPU and checkout writes time out.
incidents.constraint: Search must stay under 200 ms p95 without slowing checkout writes.
incidents.question: What should serve product search?

choices.label: Serve search from an inverted index of title terms
choices.resultBody: The index maps each term like 'boots' straight to its 18k product IDs, so a query reads one posting list instead of scanning 40M rows; the primary drops back to checkout duty.

choices.label: Add a standard B-tree index on the product title column
choices.resultBody: A B-tree is sorted by the title's first characters, so a leading % wildcard cannot seek into it; the planner still scans all 40M rows per search.

choices.label: Cache each query's results in Redis for ten minutes
choices.resultTitle: The long tail misses the cache
choices.resultBody: Only 12% of searches repeat within 10 minutes, so 88% still fall through to the ILIKE scan and the primary stays pinned near 90% CPU.

hints: What does a leading % wildcard do to a sorted index?
Search asks 'which rows contain this word', the reverse of a row lookup.
Map each term to the list of documents that contain it.

users: 3,000 searches/s, mostly one or two words
top queries: boots, jacket, rain coat
checkout: ERROR canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)
db: pg_stat_statements: 91% of CPU time from role search_api
autovacuum on orders finished in 12 s

culprit.explanation: The Search API sends ILIKE '%boots%' queries that scan all 40M rows, and pg_stat_statements pins 91% of the primary's CPU on them. The primary and checkout are victims of that query shape.

wrongNodeFeedback.db: The primary is hot, but its own stats say whose queries burn the CPU. A bigger primary would just run the same scans.
wrongNodeFeedback.checkout: Checkout's inserts time out waiting on a busy primary; it is a victim, not the cause.
wrongNodeFeedback.users: 3,000 short searches a second is ordinary traffic. What turns each one into a 40M-row job?

incidents.title: Running shoes return zero results
incidents.brief: A sports retailer's search finds 'running shoes' but not 'run shoe' or 'Running Shoes'. The index stores raw tokens with no lowercasing or stemming, and 18% of queries return nothing.
incidents.constraint: Fix recall without re-architecting search or adding query latency.
incidents.question: How should the text be analyzed?

choices.label: Run one lowercase-and-stem analyzer at index and query time
choices.resultBody: Documents and queries now pass through the same lowercase and stemming chain, so 'Running Shoes' and 'run shoe' both become run + shoe; zero-result queries fall from 18% to 3%.

choices.label: Stem only the query text and leave the stored tokens untouched
choices.resultBody: The query 'running' becomes 'run', but the index still holds 'Running' and 'running', so previously working searches miss too and zero results climb to 21%.

choices.label: Match every query term with a fuzzy edit distance of two
choices.resultBody: Expanding each term to everything within two edits multiplies posting-list reads, so CPU jumps to 81% and 'shoe' now also matches 'shop' and 'show'.

hints: How can 'Running Shoes' and 'run shoe' become the same terms?
Tokens only match if the same rules produced them.
Apply the same analyzer chain to documents and to queries.

incidents.title: Keyword-stuffed jobs rank first
incidents.brief: A job board scores matches by raw term count. Listings repeating 'python' 60 times outrank real roles, and click-through on page one has fallen from 9% to 2%.
incidents.constraint: Keep keyword search; relevance must reward real matches, not repetition.
incidents.question: How should results be scored?

choices.label: Score with BM25: saturate repeats, weight rare terms higher
choices.resultBody: BM25's term-frequency curve flattens after a few mentions, so the 60th 'python' adds almost nothing, while a rare term like 'django' counts for more; CTR recovers to 8%.

choices.label: Sort every matching listing by posting date, newest first
choices.resultBody: Recency ignores how well a listing matches, so a new 'python-adjacent sales' post beats an exact senior Python role and spammers simply repost daily.

choices.label: Rank matches by how many applications each listing received
choices.resultBody: Listings already on page one collect the applications, so the stuffed posts that ranked first keep their lead and new relevant roles never surface.

hints: Should the 60th mention of a word count as much as the first?
A word that appears in every listing tells you little.
Use a score that saturates term frequency and weights rare terms.

incidents.title: One term shard runs every query
incidents.brief: A log platform shards its 2B-document index by term. Every query touching 'error' lands on one shard at 97% CPU, and multi-term queries ship huge posting lists between shards to intersect.
incidents.constraint: Add shards without any one of them becoming the hot spot.
incidents.question: How should the index be partitioned?

choices.label: Shard by document ID and scatter each query to all shards
choices.resultBody: Each of the 16 shards holds a slice of documents with its own local index, so 'error' is split 16 ways and intersections happen locally before a small top-k merge.

choices.label: Add three read replicas behind the hot 'e-f' term shard
choices.resultBody: Replicas split 'error' lookups four ways, but multi-term queries still pull 400M-entry posting lists across the network, and 'timeout' becomes the next 90% shard.

choices.label: Cache posting lists for the 100 hottest terms
choices.resultBody: Logs arrive at 200k lines/s, so the 'error' posting list changes every millisecond; cached copies are stale at once and the shard keeps rebuilding them.

hints: Which shard does a query for 'error AND timeout' need?
Frequent words make term-partitioned shards uneven.
Give every shard a slice of documents and merge per-shard results.

incidents.title: Page 500 takes four seconds
incidents.brief: A marketplace lets scrapers request page 500 of 20 results. Each of 12 shards must return its top 10,000 hits, and the coordinator sorts 120,000 to keep 20. p95 hits 3.8 s.
incidents.constraint: Real users rarely pass page 5; bulk exports must still work.
incidents.question: How should deep results be served?

choices.label: Cap offsets at 1,000 and page deeper with search_after cursors
choices.resultBody: A search_after cursor asks each shard only for 20 hits past the last sort key, so page 500 costs what page 1 does and the coordinator merges 240 hits instead of 120,000.

choices.label: Split the index into 24 shards so each one returns fewer hits
choices.resultBody: Every shard must still return its own top 10,000 for page 500, so 24 shards send 240,000 hits and the coordinator's sort gets twice as expensive.

choices.label: Raise the coordinator's JVM heap from 8 GB to 32 GB
choices.resultBody: The 120,000-hit sort still runs on every deep page; the larger heap only defers garbage collection into 900 ms pauses that stall the shallow queries too.

hints: How many hits must each shard return for page 500?
The cost grows with offset plus size, times the shard count.
Page from the last sort key instead of an offset.

knob.label: Max offset (from + size)
knob.question: Set the offset cap; anything deeper must page with a search_after cursor.

low.title: Real shoppers hit the wall
low.body: Users rarely pass page 5, but a cap under 200 results (page 10) turns their occasional page 6 to 10 into errors; at 20 every 'next page' click fails, about 1,400 errors a second.

high.title: Scrapers still dig deep
high.body: Above 2,000 results, offset pages stay deep enough to hurt: at the 10,000 default each of 12 shards returns 10,000 hits and the coordinator sorts 120,000 to keep 20.

good.title: Every page costs about the same
good.body: A cap near 1,000 covers every real user's pages 1 to 50, deeper requests switch to search_after, and the coordinator merges about 12,000 hits instead of 120,000, so p95 falls to roughly 150 ms.

incidents.title: Prices in search drift from the DB
incidents.brief: The listings API writes Postgres, then calls the search index. When index calls time out, 0.4% of 90M listings keep stale prices, and buyers click $40 items that now cost $65.
incidents.constraint: Search may lag the database by seconds but must never lose an update.
incidents.question: How should changes reach the index?

choices.label: Stream the database changelog through a queue to indexers
choices.resultBody: CDC reads committed rows from the Postgres WAL into a durable queue, and indexers replay them with retries, so no update is lost and search trails the database by about 2 s.

choices.label: Retry each failed index write three times inside the request
choices.resultTitle: Stale prices slow to a trickle
choices.resultBody: Most timed-out index calls now succeed on a retry, so new stale listings drop by 75%. But seller saves wait up to 3 s whenever the index slows, and busy API threads have climbed to 70%.

choices.label: Rebuild the full index from Postgres every night
choices.resultBody: A 90M-row nightly rebuild loads the primary for hours, and any price changed at 9 am stays wrong in search until the next night's run.

hints: What happens if the API crashes between the two writes?
The database already records every committed change in order.
Feed the index from the database's change stream, not the app.

incidents.title: Docs search reads from disk on every query
incidents.brief: Stackdocs runs one OpenSearch node with 8 GB RAM and a 4 GB heap. New API reference pages grew the index to 9 GB, so queries now read from disk: 3,000 IOPS, p95 2.8 s.
incidents.constraint: Search must recover today; the index grows about 1 GB a year and traffic is a steady 300 searches/s.
incidents.question: What brings search latency back?

choices.label: Upsize to a 32 GB RAM node so the index fits in page cache

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A 9 GB index on one node just needs enough RAM to cache it; sharding solves a size problem this index does not have.

choices.resultTitle: The whole index lives in memory again
choices.resultBody: Lucene reads segments through the OS page cache, not the JVM heap. With 32 GB of RAM and the heap still at 4 GB, all 9 GB of segments stay cached, disk reads fall to about 40 IOPS and p95 to 60 ms. Cost: about $180 more a month, with years of headroom.

choices.label: Split the index into six primaries on a new three-node cluster
choices.resultTitle: Right-sized in two weeks, not today
choices.resultBody: Three nodes would eventually cache the index between them, but provisioning the cluster and reindexing takes the team about two weeks while p95 stays at 2.8 s. The result costs three times as much and fans every query out to six small shards.

choices.label: Raise the JVM heap from 4 GB to 6 GB so more of the index fits
choices.resultTitle: Less page cache, more disk reads
choices.resultBody: The heap does not hold the segments. Growing it squeezes the page cache on the 8 GB box from about 4 GB to 2 GB, so more queries miss memory, the disk stays pinned at its 3,000 IOPS limit and p95 climbs to 4.1 s.

hints: Compare the index size with the memory left over after the heap.
Lucene relies on the operating system to keep segment files in memory.
This index is small and grows slowly; it doesn't need more nodes, it needs room.

incidents.title: Search goes dark during a node patch
incidents.brief: Product search now runs on one OpenSearch node with no replicas. A kernel patch rebooted it, and every search returned 503 for 6 minutes during the lunch peak.
incidents.constraint: Patches ship monthly, and checkout's Postgres primary must never serve search again.
incidents.question: How does search survive losing a node?

choices.label: Add a second node and one replica of every shard
choices.resultBody: With a replica of every shard on node 2, the cluster promotes the copies when node 1 reboots and searches keep answering; patch one node at a time. Cost: about $150 a month and double the indexing writes.

choices.label: Fall back to ILIKE queries on Postgres when search is down
choices.resultBody: The next reboot sends 3,000 ILIKE scans a second back to Postgres, CPU hits 96% and checkout writes time out alongside search, the outage you just fixed.

choices.label: Snapshot the index to S3 hourly and restore it after failures
choices.resultBody: A snapshot protects data, not uptime: the lone node still leaves search dark on every reboot, and a lost disk would now mean a 25-minute restore of 40M products.

hints: How many copies of each shard exist right now?
A node reboot should not be a search outage.
Keep a copy of every shard on a different machine.

incidents.title: Old prices win the race into search
incidents.brief: The CDC feed runs 8 indexers on one unordered queue. When a seller edits a price twice within a second, the older event sometimes lands last: 9,000 listings show the previous price.
incidents.constraint: Indexing must keep up with 12,000 changes/s; search may lag by seconds.
incidents.question: How do you stop an older change overwriting a newer one?

choices.label: Index with external versions set to each change's WAL LSN
choices.resultBody: Each write carries its commit's LSN as an external version, so the index refuses any event older than the one it holds; late deliveries become no-ops and all 8 indexers keep running. Cost: a logged version conflict per race.

choices.label: Run a single indexer so every event applies in order
choices.resultBody: One indexer applies about 2,000 changes/s against 12,000 arriving, so its lag grows by minutes every minute and soon every price in search is stale.

choices.label: Re-read the listing from Postgres before each index write
choices.resultBody: Two indexers can read the row at different moments and still write in the wrong order, and the extra 12,000 reads/s push the primary from 41% to 68% CPU.

hints: Two indexers can finish their work in either order.
The database already stamps every commit with an increasing position.
Let the index refuse a write older than the one it already has.

incidents.title: Index retries exhaust the Listings API
incidents.brief: The inline retries held until tonight's segment merge slowed index writes to 2 s. Every save now retries three times, API threads sit at 400/400, and seller saves fail with 503.
incidents.constraint: Search may lag by seconds but must never lose an update; saves can't wait on search.
incidents.question: What takes the index off the save path for good?

choices.label: Write an outbox row in the same transaction; relay it to search
choices.resultBody: The save commits the listing and an outbox row together, and a relay worker feeds the index with retries off the request path; saves fall to 90 ms and no update is lost. Cost: a $60 relay worker and seconds of lag.

choices.label: Skip the index write whenever it takes over 200 ms
choices.resultBody: Saves recover to 100 ms, but every write skipped during the merge is simply gone, so stale listings keep climbing past 600,000 with no way to know which ones.

choices.label: Double the Listings API pods to hold more in-flight retries
choices.resultBody: Twice the pods send twice the concurrent retries into an index already slowed by its merge, so index writes stretch to 4 s and the new threads fill up within minutes.

hints: The retries hid the problem; the save still waits on search.
The database commit is the only write that must succeed synchronously.
Record the change in the same transaction and deliver it later.
